standards.title: Springs for anything a finger drives
standards.rule: Animate drags, flicks, swipes and any other gesture the user can interrupt or reverse mid-motion with a spring, not with a fixed-duration transition or @keyframes.
standards.why: Springs start from the current value and carry velocity through an interruption, while timing curves restart; a pre-scripted, fixed-duration animation cannot respond to new input. Non-gesture UI that is triggered rapidly only needs a CSS transition (STD-springs-gestures-15).

standards.title: Define springs by damping and response
standards.rule: Specify each spring with two designer parameters, damping ratio (or bounce) and response (or duration), rather than mass, stiffness and damping, and never treat response as a fixed duration.
standards.why: Apple deliberately replaced the physics triplet with these two designer-friendly parameters, and Emil recommends the duration-and-bounce form as easier to reason about. A spring has no fixed duration: its settle time emerges from the parameters.

values.damping-ratio: 1.0 = critically damped, no bounce, smooth settle. < 1.0 = overshoots and oscillates.
values.response: how quickly the value reaches the target, in seconds

standards.title: Every animation can be grabbed mid-flight
standards.rule: Make every animation the user triggers or touches interruptible and redirectable at any moment: a user can grab a moving element mid-flight and reverse it, and a closing modal or sheet that is grabbed again follows the finger instead of finishing its close first.
standards.why: Interruptibility is the single most important principle, because the thought and the gesture happen in parallel; for anything a finger touches it is the baseline, not polish.

standards.title: Carry velocity through a reversal
standards.rule: When a gesture reverses direction mid-animation, carry the current velocity through the re-target instead of cutting to a new animation (on the web, use a spring library that re-targets from the current velocity).
standards.why: Replacing one animation with another at a reversal creates a velocity discontinuity, a 'brick wall'; iOS avoids it natively with additive animations.

standards.title: Project the flick, then snap

Performance Rules: 'CSS variables are inheritable'
'Don't drive child transforms via a CSS variable on the parent'

review.message: Drag offset set through a CSS variable: write element.style.transform on the dragged element instead.

standards.title: No re-render per drag frame
standards.rule: Update drag and other per-frame values without a React render per frame: write to ref.current.style or a Reanimated shared value, never setState from a gesture or scroll handler.
standards.why: The drag must not drop frames, and one React render per frame is the single biggest cause of jank in React Native apps.

sources.evidence: Drag gesture: 'Not losing frames while dragging is a good start'; 'Dragging was done without any re-renders'
'React re-renders every frame | Write to ref.current.style, not state'
6. Keep it off the JS thread: 'Never setState from a gesture or scroll handler.'

standards.title: Derive linked visuals from the drag
standards.rule: Drive everything that follows a drag (backdrop opacity, the background's scale and corner radius) from the same drag value or drag progress, not from separate animations.
standards.why: Values tied to drag progress stay in sync and cost nothing extra.

values.example: Dragging the drawer down by 40% will change the border radius to 60% of its max value

sources.evidence: Background animation: 'all the values are based on the drag progress'
Bottom sheet: 'The backdrop derives from the same value, so it's always in sync and costs nothing'

standards.title: Swipe to dismiss toasts and drawers
standards.rule: Let people dismiss toasts and drawers by swiping or dragging them away, on touch devices and on desktop.
standards.why: People are already used to swiping notifications away on their devices; the drawer Vaul replaced lacked drag-to-dismiss.

sources.evidence: 'Another Sonner feature is the swipe gesture ... You can also swipe on desktop.'
'it lacked drag-to-dismiss functionality'

standards.title: Leave along the path you entered
standards.rule: Make a dismissable element leave along the same path and edge it entered from, so its swipe-to-dismiss direction matches its entrance.
standards.why: If something disappears one way, we expect it to emerge from where it came; symmetric paths make swipe-to-dismiss feel obvious.

sources.evidence: 7. Spatial consistency: 'Enter and exit along the same path.'
6. 'Exit the way it entered. ... Symmetric paths are what make swipe-to-dismiss feel obvious.'
'Because it comes from and leaves in the same direction, it creates spatial consistency'
'Spatial consistency: toast enters and exits from the same direction'
'Dismissable surfaces (toasts, sheets) that exit a different way than they entered → symmetric paths'

standards.title: Feedback on press, commit on release
standards.rule: Show press feedback the instant the pointer or finger goes down, and commit the action on release.
standards.why: Waiting for click or touch-up to show feedback feels dead and reads as lag even at 0ms.

values.react-native: feedback on press-in, commit on press-out

sources.evidence: 1. Response: 'Respond on pointer-down, not on release.'; 10. 'Tap: highlight on touch-down (instant), commit on touch-up.'
5. Tap feels laggy: 'Feedback on release instead of press.'
7. Press, not hover: 'Feedback on press-in, commit on press-out.'

standards.title: Forgiving taps with hysteresis
standards.rule: Give tap targets about 10px of hysteresis or hit padding and let a tap be cancelled by dragging away and restored by dragging back; on React Native set pressRetentionOffset.
standards.why: A finger drifting a few pixels should not cancel a press the user meant.

sources.evidence: 10. Gesture design details: 'Add ~10px of hysteresis/hit padding around the target, and allow cancel-by-dragging-away and back.'
7. Press, not hover: 'pressRetentionOffset so a finger drifting a few pixels doesn't cancel a press the user meant.'
Press feedback: 'pressRetentionOffset stops a slight finger drift from cancelling.'

standards.title: Recognize gestures continuously, in parallel
standards.rule: Track every plausible gesture in parallel from the first move and cancel the losers once intent is clear; do not use recognizers that only report a final state (swipeleft-type events).
standards.why: Final-state recognizers throw away the continuous tracking you need for feedback.

sources.evidence: 10. 'Detect all plausible gestures in parallel from the first move ... Avoid recognizers that only report a final state'

review.message: Final-state swipe recognizer: track the pointer continuously (a pan) and decide on release.

standards.title: Double-tap only where it exists
standards.rule: Add double-tap detection only where a double-tap action exists.
standards.why: Double-tap detection unavoidably delays single taps.

sources.evidence: 10. 'Minimize disambiguation delays. Double-tap detection unavoidably delays single taps'

standards.title: Remove latency from the input path
standards.rule: Audit every latency on the input path (debounces, artificial timers, transition waits, the ~300ms tap delay) and remove anything that is not essential.
standards.why: The moment lag appears, the feeling of directness falls off a cliff; anything non-essential on the input path is a regression.

sources.evidence: 1. Response — kill latency: 'Be vigilant about every latency.'

standards.title: Hint in the gesture's direction
standards.rule: Make intermediate frames point toward the outcome (for example growing up and out toward the finger) rather than interpolating blindly to the end state.
standards.why: Humans predict a final state from a trajectory.

sources.evidence: 8. Hint in the direction of the gesture

standards.title: Keep per-frame movement imperceptible
standards.rule: Keep each frame's positional change below the perception threshold so motion does not strobe.
standards.why: Smoothness is about what is in the frames, not just the frame rate.

sources.evidence: 11. Frame-level smoothness: 'Keep the per-frame positional change below the perception threshold to avoid strobing.'

standards.title: Mirror easing on reversible transitions
standards.rule: On a reversible transition, mirror the easing so the return path matches the outbound path, using inverse cubic-bézier control points for the two directions.
standards.why: Part of spatial consistency: the outbound path should match the return path.

sources.evidence: 7. Spatial consistency: 'Mirror the easing on reversible transitions'

standards.title: Spring-smooth decorative mouse tracking
standards.rule: Pass decorative mouse-tracking values through a spring (Motion's useSpring) instead of tying the visual directly to the pointer position.
standards.why: Tying visual changes directly to mouse position feels artificial because it lacks motion; a spring adds momentum.

sources.evidence: Spring-based mouse interactions
'Mouse interactions: interpolate with useSpring rather than tying value directly to mouse position'

standards.title: No decorative springs on functional displays
standards.rule: Spring-smooth pointer-tied motion only when it is decorative; keep it off functional displays such as data charts.
standards.why: The spring effect works only because it is decorative: for a functional graph no animation would be better, and the useSpring graph interaction is meant for illustrations, not functional graphs like stock charts.

sources.evidence: 'If this were a functional graph in a banking app, no animation would be better.'
Mouse interactions: 'Only do this when the motion is decorative.'
'this type of interaction is meant for illustrations, not functional graphs like stock charts'

standards.title: Translucent chrome over scrolling content
standards.rule: Build nav bars, toolbars and sheets as translucent layers (backdrop-filter: blur() over a semi-transparent background) with content scrolling underneath, not as opaque bars that take a fixed strip.
standards.why: Translucent materials act as a floating functional layer that brings structure without stealing focus.

values.example-light-toolbar: background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6); backdrop-filter: blur(20px) saturate(180%); border-top: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.4)

sources.evidence: 12. Materials & depth: 'Build nav/toolbars/sheets as translucent layers'

standards.title: Material weight encodes hierarchy
standards.rule: Use darker, heavier materials to separate structural regions such as sidebars, and lighter materials to draw attention to interactive elements such as buttons.
standards.why: Material weight encodes hierarchy.

sources.evidence: 12. 'Material weight encodes hierarchy'

standards.title: Never stack light glass on light glass
standards.rule: Never place a light translucent surface on top of another light translucent surface.
standards.why: Legibility collapses.

sources.evidence: 12. 'Never stack a light translucent surface on another — legibility collapses.'

standards.title: Bigger surfaces read as thicker
standards.rule: Give bigger translucent surfaces a stronger blur and a deeper shadow than small chips.
standards.why: Bigger surfaces should read as thicker material.

sources.evidence: 12. 'Bigger surfaces should read as thicker: stronger blur + a deeper shadow than small chips.'

standards.title: Modal surfaces dim and push back
standards.rule: Pair a modal task's surface with a dimming scrim and push the background back or down, and with stacked sheets dim and push back each parent layer progressively.
standards.why: Dim to focus: the scrim and the pushed-back background show that the task has taken over.

sources.evidence: 12. 'Dim to focus, separate to keep flow. A modal task pairs the surface with a dimming scrim and pushes the background back/down. ... For stacked sheets, progressively dim and push back each parent layer.'

standards.title: Non-blocking panels skip the scrim
standards.rule: Give a parallel, non-blocking panel translucency and an offset but no scrim.
standards.why: Separate to keep flow: without a scrim the flow is not broken.

sources.evidence: 12. 'A parallel, non-blocking panel uses translucency and offset without a scrim so the flow isn't broken.'

standards.title: Vibrant text over translucent surfaces
standards.rule: Over blurred or translucent surfaces, set text in higher contrast, a slightly heavier weight and a small letter-spacing increase, not flat gray.
standards.why: Vibrancy keeps text legible over changing backgrounds.

sources.evidence: 12. 'Vibrancy keeps text legible over changing backgrounds.'

standards.title: Color on a solid layer
standards.rule: Put color on a solid layer, not on the translucent foreground.
standards.why: Part of keeping content legible over translucent materials.

sources.evidence: 12. 'Put color on a solid layer, not the translucent foreground.'

standards.title: Scroll edge effects, not dividers
standards.rule: Separate floating chrome from scrolling content with a small fading blur or gradient mask, only where the floating UI actually overlaps content, instead of a 1px border under a sticky header.
standards.why: Scroll edge effects, not hard dividers.

sources.evidence: 12. 'Scroll edge effects, not hard dividers. Instead of a 1px border under a sticky header, fade a small blur/gradient mask'

review.message: 1px divider under a sticky header: fade a scroll-edge blur or gradient mask where content passes under it.

standards.title: Materialize glass, don't just fade
standards.rule: Bring glass or blur surfaces in and out by animating blur radius and scale together, not with a plain opacity fade.
standards.why: The surface then reads as a real material arriving rather than a plain opacity fade.

sources.evidence: 12. 'Materialize, don't just fade.'

standards.title: Solid surfaces under reduced transparency
standards.rule: Under prefers-reduced-transparency: reduce, make translucent surfaces frostier or solid by raising the background opacity and dropping the blur.
standards.why: Components should respond to the three independent signals (reduced motion, reduced transparency, increased contrast) with the fallback built in.

sources.evidence: 14. 'prefers-reduced-transparency: reduce — make translucent surfaces frostier/solid: raise background opacity, drop the blur.'
14. 'Respond to three independent signals and bake them into your components'

standards.title: Near-solid glass under increased contrast
standards.rule: Under prefers-contrast: more, give translucent surfaces a near-solid background and a defined, contrasting border.
standards.why: It is one of the three independent signals the source says to bake into components.

sources.evidence: 14. 'prefers-contrast: more — near-solid backgrounds with a defined, contrasting border.'

standards.title: Feedback fires on the causal event
standards.rule: Fire motion, sound and haptic feedback on the actual causal event (the toggle flipping, the item snapping home, the detent catching), not when an animation finishes, and match its character to the physicality of the action.
standards.why: It must be obvious what caused the feedback.

values.react-native-tab-example: Haptics.selectionAsync() on the press, not when the pill lands

sources.evidence: 13. Multimodal feedback: '1. Causality — it must be obvious what caused the feedback.'
8. Haptics: 'Fire it at the causal moment — the detent catching — not when the animation finishes.'
Tab indicator: 'Fire Haptics.selectionAsync() on the press, not when the pill lands.'

standards.title: Visual, sound and haptic share a frame
standards.rule: Fire the visual, the sound and the haptic in the same frame; never let a CSS transition lag the audio or haptic.
standards.why: Latency between them destroys the illusion, and a haptic that lags its animation reads as a glitch, not as feedback.

sources.evidence: 13. '2. Harmony — the visual, the sound, and the haptic must fire on the same frame.'
8. Haptics: 'Same frame as the visual. A haptic that lags its animation reads as a glitch, not as feedback.'

standards.title: Haptics and sound only when meaningful
standards.rule: Reserve haptics and sound for meaningful moments (success, error, commit, snap), and fire at most one haptic per user action: never on scroll, never per frame, never on an entrance animation the user did not cause.
standards.why: Over-feedback trains users to ignore all of it; used everywhere, users turn haptics off.

sources.evidence: 13. '3. Utility — add feedback only where it earns its place.'
8. Haptics: 'One per user action. Never on scroll, never per frame, never on an entrance animation the user didn't cause.'

standards.title: Haptics never stand alone
standards.rule: Never make a haptic the only feedback; pair it with a visual that stands on its own.
standards.why: Haptics are off system-wide for many users and silent on most Android hardware.

sources.evidence: 8. Haptics: 'Never the only feedback. Haptics are off system-wide for many users, and silent on most Android hardware.'

standards.title: Blur or stretch very fast motion
standards.rule: For very fast motion, add a subtle motion blur or stretch along the direction of travel rather than moving a hard, sharp edge.
standards.why: A subtle blur or stretch encodes speed and reads better than a hard sharp streak; smoothness is about what is in the frames, not just the frame rate.

sources.evidence: For very fast motion, a subtle motion blur / stretch encodes speed and reads better than a hard sharp streak.
